title: Why Does God Allow This?
overview: The prophet Habakkuk asks God why injustice goes unchecked, and the answer, that a brutal empire is on its way, only deepens his question.

parts.label: A cry about injustice (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Habakkuk complains that violence and crooked courts surround him while the LORD seems not to act. Most readers take this as wrongdoing inside his own nation of Judah, where the law has lost its force and the powerful hem in the honest.

parts.label: An unbelievable answer (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: The LORD replies that he is raising up the Babylonians, the rising empire of that time; on the traditional reading, they come to punish the wrongs Habakkuk just described. Christians later heard verse 5 again, because in the book of Acts Paul quotes it as a warning to people who dismiss the message about Jesus.

parts.label: A portrait of the invaders (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: Leopards, wolves hungry at dusk, swooping eagles and a scorching desert wind all picture an army that is fast, fierce and answers to no one but itself. Earthen ramps were mounds of dirt piled against city walls so attackers could get over, and the section ends by saying their real god is their own strength.

parts.label: Habakkuk pushes back (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: He holds on to what he believes about God, that he is eternal, holy and steady as a rock, and accepts that the Babylonians are sent to punish. But that makes his question sharper: how can a pure God stay silent while the more wicked swallow up people less wicked than themselves?

parts.label: Nations caught like fish (vv. 14-17)
parts.note: He pictures the conqueror as a fisherman hauling in whole peoples with hooks and nets, as if they had no one to protect them. Offering sacrifices to his net means treating his weapons and military power as the source of his rich life, and the chapter ends on an open question: will this go on forever?

disagreement: Interpreters differ on whether the violence Habakkuk first complains about (vv. 2-4) is wrongdoing inside Judah, which most traditional readers assume, or oppression by a foreign power, which some scholars argue, and this shapes how the whole exchange is understood.
think: Habakkuk's answer made his question harder rather than easier; have you ever met an explanation for suffering that left you more troubled than before, and what did you do with it?
